technique: the turn — the exact line where picture becomes meaning, and how the poem earns it
lesson: Today we work on one thing: the turn. The turn is the exact line where a poem stops showing you a picture and starts telling you what it means. This poem spends most of its length on the body waking up. "the honest weight of you pressed down." "one foot gone looking, finding the plank floor cold." Those are plain physical facts. Then the poem turns. "No column waits out here to add you up or hold / what's owed against your name." That is the meaning. The waking body owes nothing today. It works because you feel the body first, so when the meaning comes you already believe it. You earned it through the cold foot and the breath. Try this: write five lines of pure physical detail, then one line that says what it adds up to. The second time, listen for how the whole poem builds toward "So — up!" Here is the poem.
poem:
Breath first — the long pull of it, cold at the edges,
the chest filling like a bucket left out overnight.
Then weight, the honest weight of you pressed down
into the mattress, bones remembering their ground.
Warmth under the blanket you're half out of already,
one foot gone looking, finding the plank floor cold
and glad of it, the way the body wakes to a number
it can trust — this much heat, this much ache, this much done.
No column waits out here to add you up or hold
what's owed against your name; the day asks plainer things.
Pale light now at the sill, the frost drawn thin,
November laying its gray hand flat across the hills.

The window's doing something ordinary and good out there, and it won't wait around for you to come see it—

So — up!
